Its campaign was led by Lynn Dekleva , then a lobbyist at the American Chemistry Council ,” The New York Times’ Hiroko Tabuchi reports.

— “Dr. Dekleva is now at the E.P.A. in a crucial job: She runs an office that has the authority to approve new chemicals for use. Earlier she spent 32 years at Dupont , the chemical maker, before joining the E.P.A. in the first Trump administration.”

— “The American Chemistry Council is also seeking to change the agency’s approval process for new chemicals and speed up E.P.A.’s safety reviews. That review process is a key part of Dr. Dekelva’s purview at the agency. AN APPLE A DAY: The president this morning hammered Apple after the tech giant’s shareholders voted against axing company diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives that conservatives have railed against.
— “APPLE SHOULD GET RID OF DEI RULES, NOT JUST MAKE ADJUSTMENTS TO THEM,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social , going on to call such programs a “hoax” that have “BEEN VERY BAD FOR OUR COUNTRY.”

— Apple is one of just a few major corporations that has not retreated from diversity programs — a trend that only accelerated after Trump took office and became a driving crusade of the first month of his administration. Apple had urged investors to oppose the anti-DEI proposal, though CEO Tim Cook said after the vote that the company may still need to make tweaks to those programs “as the legal landscape changes,” according to the Associated Press .

— The fate of the proposed changes was already unclear before new Attorney General Pam Bondi last month signaled the rollback of a nearly decadeold enforcement crackdown in the name of shifting the department’s resources and reducing weaponization — an apparent inconsistency that several comments seized upon.

— “The Department’s proposal would cast arguably the widest FARA registration net in the law’s history at a time when the Attorney General is ordering a prosecutorial focus on FARA’s core,” lawyers from Caplin & Drysdale wrote in their comment on the proposed regulations, arguing that one of DOJ’s key changes “would run counter to a basic intent of the Bondi Memorandum.”

— “Rather than providing the actual ‘test,’ however, the proposed language simply lists a set of non-exhaustive factors that may or may not be among those the Department would turn to,” the law firm Sandler Reiff Lamb Rosenstein & Birkenstock wrote in its comment .

— The provision’s critics ranged from business groups including the Association for Accessible Medicines and the American Petroleum Institute to organizations representing journalists and nonprofits, who warned that rather than undertake the administrative burden of determining whether or not they are required to register under FARA, “potentially stifling legitimate ‘political activity,’ as defined in the statute,” API argued.

— Moreover, “in many situations, organizations do not have time or resources to request an advisory opinion. Waiting for an advisory opinion before taking an action can so delay the action or speech that its meaning is then lost — chilling First Amendment protected rights,” the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law warned .

— An advocacy group representing journalists went even further. “Were FARA enforced consistent with its expansive and ambiguous text, those actions would flatly violate the First Amendment,” the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press said in its comments .

— AAM and the Pennsylvania-based biopharmaceutical company CSL raised concerns about what the FARA changes — if adopted as proposed — might mean for trade groups whose membership includes foreign-based companies. The comments came after FARA-related pressure from lawmakers last year that prompted the Biotechnology Innovation Organization to drop one of its China-based members.

— Another commenter had first-hand experience with running afoul of FARA. Pierre Girgis , a dual U.S.-Egyptian citizen who pleaded guilty in 2022 to a “failure to label” FARA violation, wrote in to opine about how FARA enforcement has tended to “come down hard on certain private individuals (often those tied to adversarial regimes or lacking political clout), while similar foreign influence activities by insiders or allies are frequently overlooked.”

But that influence has eroded in recent years alongside its relationship with traditional GOP allies, putting the lobbying giant in a tough spot to fight tariffs and push tax priorities at the start of a second Trump administration,” NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno writes.

— “As the president has launched an aggressive tariff strategy at the start of his second term, the Chamber’s objections don’t appear to be going far. And while the 2017 tax cuts were a huge victory for the business community and its advocates, the Chamber is entering lobbying efforts this year on the heels of a House investigation into donations to the Chamber’s foundation from left-leaning organizations — led by House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith .”

— While a source told NOTUS that “the Chamber isn’t in the conversation” about the tax bill, the group’s top lobbyist pushed back on the suggestion. “Whoever said that might not be in the same rooms that we’re in,” said Neil Bradley , who on Wednesday hosted the GOP leader of the Senate Finance Committee as well as a member of the Ways and Means Committee at a Chamber-organized tax summit.

— “The waning influence of the Chamber has been a source of discussion on K Street for some time, but often in hushed tones on background or off the record. The reticence to outright write off the Chamber indicates its influence has perhaps not waned beyond repair, but four more years of President Donald Trump and a Republican Party more beholden to MAGA than traditional conservative principles will undoubtedly be a challenge unlike any other in the institution’s 113-year history.”

FIRST IN PI: Geoffrey Pyatt , the top U.S. diplomat for energy issues under former President Joe Biden, is joining global strategic advisory firm McLarty Associates to launch a new practice focused on helping companies navigate the increasingly fraught and complex geopolitical landscape for critical minerals and energy.

— Even under President Donald Trump , who has railed against the electric vehicle industry for which the critical mineral supply chain is crucial, the sector has already played a massive role in the current administration’s diplomatic priorities. Trump signed an executive order just today aimed at boosting U.S. production of rare earth minerals, an arena currently dominated by China.

— And last month’s Oval Office blow up between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was intended to be a precursor to the signing of a deal to grant U.S. access to Ukrainian rare earth minerals that are used in products like batteries and electronics. Trump told reporters this afternoon that the deal was back on track to be signed imminently.

— “Energy and critical minerals are remaking geopolitics and creating enormous economic competition and opportunity everywhere,” said Lee Feinstein , president of McLarty Associates, which was founded by former Bill Clinton chief of staff Mack McLarty and practices what it dubs “commercial diplomacy.”

— The group had a prior PAC that was last active in 2012, according to public records. The CDIA is working with Republican compliance consultant Cabell Hobbs , who serves as the PAC’s treasurer. Hobbs has worked with numerous GOP congressional members and PACs, and his involvement might signal which party the CDIA could favor with its PAC contributions.

— The Arizona Democrat-turned-independent is joining the law and lobbying firm Hogan Lovells , where she will serve as a senior counsel in the global regulatory and intellectual property practice.

— Sinema said in an interview that she will not be registering to lobby, but instead will advise businesses across industries to “understand, anticipate and influence the shifting regulatory landscape” and help them “navigate the intersection of business and government.” Daniel Winkler , a longtime Sinema aide, is joining Hogan Lovells as well.

— Though her new role with Hogan Lovells is Sinema’s most significant step into the influence industry since leaving office earlier this year, it isn’t her first. In January, Sinema joined the global advisory council at crypto exchange Coinbase alongside Chris LaCivita , President Donald Trump ’s 2024 co-campaign manager. Sinema also formed the Arizona Business Roundtable , which retained Mehlman Consulting in January to lobby on tax issues.

— Former Trump co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita , who has had a long-running feud with Roe, said in an X post on Thursday : “Today is Liberation Day for many of @jeffroe’s employees who word on the street is will be unceremoniously sacked. FARA FRIDAY: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is pressing the Justice Department to ditch its plans to let up on FARA prosecutions and other efforts to curtail illicit foreign influence campaigns, and to support legislation giving DOJ additional resources to uncover foreign influence campaigns.

— “I am deeply concerned that your recent decisions suggest a conscious effort to turn a blind eye to — if not welcome — foreign influence,” Blumenthal wrote in a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi . And far from diverting DOJ resources away from “more pressing priorities” and carrying the taint of alleged weaponization, he argued, “our current efforts at combating foreign influence are insufficient.”

— The senator pointed to an analysis this week from Responsible Statecraft that found that disclosure filings of informational materials required by FARA declined following Bondi’s February directive to limit criminal FARA prosecutions, and to his own efforts to investigate a Saudi sovereign wealth fund’s commercial investments in the U.S.

— Blumenthal pointed to the Public Investment Fund ’s efforts to stymie that probe, in part by taking its own consultants to court to prevent them from complying with Blumenthal’s subpoenas. The senator asked Bondi to support his bill that would more explicitly subject sovereign wealth funds like PIF and provide DOJ with additional civil investigative authorities.

— The move, which Beckerman said had been in the works for the better part of a year, comes as what appeared to be a grave threat for the video-sharing app’s future in the U.S. has largely receded following the passage of legislation aimed at forcing divestiture by TikTok’s Chinese parent company ByteDance or else face a ban.

— Beckerman led TikTok’s fight against a federal ban — and though his aggressive lobbying push came up short on Capitol Hill, former President Joe Biden and Trump both declined to enforce the ban. The Trump administration is still working to hash out a deal to secure a new ownership structure.

— Beckerman joined TikTok in 2020 from the Internet Association , the vaunted tech industry group he’d led since its founding in 2012. Less than two years later, the group — whose members included Google , Amazon , Facebook and Microsoft — shut its doors amid infighting and struggles to maintain its influence in Washington.

Brownstein’s revenue dipped slightly in the first quarter of 2025, to $16.8 million, while Akin’s jumped up to $16.4 million, according to figures shared by the firms.

— The fly-in “comes as Republicans work to finalize the tax portions of their party-line megabill before a committee vote as soon as next week. Congressional leaders and the administration are working to decide what parts of the climate bill survive, get tweaked or die. … House Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) has said the fate of the Inflation Reduction Act is one of a few sticking points that the committee still has to parse out.”
— Meanwhile, the Koch-backed Americans for Prosperity launched its own salvo against the IRA tax credits with a new ad buy blasting the incentives as “reckless spending on green fantasies.”
— “Eliminating Joe Biden ‘s Green New Deal helps pay for President Trump’s tax cuts,” the group argued in a 30-second spot that will run within the Beltway .

— The weeklong lobbying blitz featured a reception at CTA’s Capitol Hill townhome, visits to the Hill itself and meetings with administration officials. CTA has also launched a six-figure ad buy in Beltway news outlets and at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport .

— “‘It’s a bit of an experiment,’ Ed Brzytwa , CTA’s vice president of international trade, told POLITICO in an interview ahead of the event. ‘We’re trying to engage [with the administration] as best as we can.’”

— “CTA, which sponsors the largest tech convention in the country — the annual CES in Las Vegas — has been more overt than most in critiquing Trump’s trade policies, with CEO Gary Shapiro publicly swiping at the president’s tariffs when they were first announced in the Rose Garden in early April.” But the association “will have to balance publicly pushing its members’ concerns against the tariffs while remaining seemingly aligned with the president.”

FIRST IN PI — FOREIGN STAKEHOLDERS TRIP UP ILFA LOBBYISTS AGAIN: A lobbying firm representing the International Legal Finance Association again is correcting a failure to disclose that the association has foreign entities that have a direct interest in its lobbying activities, Daniel reports.

— When S-3 Group filed its LD-1 lobbying registration form in January for ILFA, it identified six foreign entities with that interest. However, when it recently filed its LD-2 disclosure form for the first quarter, it checked the box that said there were no foreign stakeholders.

— The lack of disclosure comes as there are increasing concerns that foreign litigation financing could be used to undermine American interests. Several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at forcing more transparency around the practice — something the U.S. Chamber of Commerce has also lobbied hard for.

— The head of DOJ’s FARA Unit reaffirmed last year that foreign litigation funding is an area of interest in terms of the unit’s enforcement priorities, though it is unclear if that will remain the case under Attorney General Pam Bondi .

— At the start of this year, ILFA switched lobbying firms and is now represented by S-3 Group. The two people lobbying on its behalf at S-3 Group, Kristi Remington and Craig Kalkut , also previously represented them at West Front Strategies , which is no longer retained by ILFA. When West Front filed quarterly disclosures for the group, it disclosed the interest of foreign entities in the work.

— Hillsdale last month retained Williams and Jensen to lobby on “specific threats to the institutional and financial independence of the college, primarily related to the higher education endowment tax,” the filing shows. The team of lobbyists working on the account includes Dan Ziegler , who served as House Speaker Mike Johnson ’s top policy aide before returning to the firm in March .
— The school’s president, Larry Arnn , ripped the House proposal in an op-ed last week that called the changes “not merely bad policy,” but “a profound inversion of the American idea.”

— Bartlett was most recently a deputy assistant secretary of State during the Biden administration and has served as a spokesperson for several top Democrats in Congress over the years. Baum joins from American Veterinary Medical Association , where she was director of strategic communications, and is an alum of the first Trump administration.

— So in many ways, this was a long time coming for a firm that brought in more than $67 million in lobbying revenues last year. FIRST IN PI — NYT HIRES BROWNSTEIN: The New York Times has registered to lobby for the first time in more than a decade. The news giant has retained K Street heavyweight Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to represent it on a range of issues affecting the industry, from encroachments on press freedoms to the threats posed by artificial intelligence.

— The Times’ parent company first hired Brownstein last year, but the firm’s work didn’t trigger lobbying registration requirements until April, according to a spokesperson for the company and a draft disclosure filing shared with PI. More than half a dozen lobbyists are listed as working on the account for Brownstein: Republicans Marc Lampkin , Will Moschella and Greta Joynes and Democrats Al Mottur , Alice Lugo , Rob Robillard and John Menges .

— One issue drawing the paper off the lobbying sidelines is the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence and the thorny issues it poses for news organizations. The Times, for example, introduced a suite of AI tools for internal use earlier this year. And many news outlets ( including the Times , POLITICO and parent company Axel Springer ) have partnered with AI companies on licensing deals and consumer-facing products.

— But NYT is also one of several publishers facing off in court against ChatGPT creator OpenAI or other AI companies accused of copyright infringement for using outlets’ content to train its models without permission or compensation.

— In a speech last month that was republished as an essay in the Times, Sulzberger took note of President Donald Trump ’s escalating pressure campaign against news outlets already in his second term — from curtailing access to certain mainstream outlets in favor of friendlier partisan ones to suing, seeking to defund or opening federal probes of others and calling for the jailing of reporters.

— Elsewhere on the Hill, more than 1,000 advocates with the Alzheimer’s Association were in town today for a fly-in aimed at winning additional investments in Alzheimer’s and dementia research. — There are a few reconciliation-focused fly-ins this week as well. State leaders with Americans for Prosperity are in town to lobby Hill offices on permanently renewing the 2017 tax cuts. — And the National Federation of Independent Business has flown in small business leaders to lobby for maintaining the House-passed reconciliation bill’s permanent extension of the 20 percent pass-through deduction. FRIENDS IN HIGH PLACES: Gaurav Srivastava, the Indian American businessperson who last year had major donations to Democrats frozen or returned after allegations he had posed as a spy for the CIA, now appears to be trying to curry favor with top Republicans, Daniel L. reports.

— Srivastava on Thursday posted a photo he recently took with Vice President JD Vance , adding in a caption, “Pleasure seeing Vice President @JDVance during last week’s event in #WashingtonDC as we work towards strengthening America’s future!”

— The photo was taken at the performance of “Les Misérables” at the Kennedy Center that President Donald Trump and Vance attended along with a slew of other senior administration and Republican figures.
— Earlier this year, Srivastava also had lunch with Hunter Biden , according to photos the Daily Mail snapped .

— In 2023, the FBI reportedly began investigating Srivastava and where he got his money. Srivastava has been engaged in a long-running battle with Dutch oil trader Niels Troost after their business relationship went sour. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the status of the investigation.

BLASE PRESSED ON PPP LOAN: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-N.J.) evidently reads PI because on Wednesday she asked Brian Blase , president of the Paragon Health Institute , about our reporting on him receiving a PPP loan that he didn’t repay, Daniel reports.

— In a House Budget Committee hearing about Medicaid reform, Watson Coleman sharply questioned Blase about the loan for Blase Policy Strategies LLC and why he didn’t pay it back. Blase, a prominent Republican advocate of Medicaid cuts, told her the loan had been forgiven since it was part of the PPP program (in line with most PPP loans). She also asked him about his purchase of a nearly $700,000 house soon after getting the loan, leading Blase to say it was because of his family moving.

(The megabill still has to clear the House, where a new set of challenges awaits , but the package nevertheless appears poised to squeak through.)

— A deal between Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) to shorten the duration of a moratorium on state and local enforcement of artificial intelligence regulations also collapsed overnight. The chamber voted overwhelmingly to remove the moratorium from the bill altogether, in a blow to tech companies, business groups and venture capitalists.

— Conservative efforts to make steeper Medicaid cuts never came up for a vote. And though a crackdown on state provider taxes that drew fierce opposition from hospitals remains in the bill (albeit with a new delay in implementation added over the weekend), Republicans did double the pot of funding to help rural hospitals, POLITICO’s David Lim reports.

— Among the losers: The fitness industry’s push for coverage of gym and fitness memberships by HSAs — which The Health & Fitness Association argued would have “honor[ed] the promise of Make America Healthy Again” — fell short. And of course, hospitals remain livid over the Senate bill’s Medicaid changes.

GONE BUT NOT FORGOTTEN: The removal of an effort to block state and local AI regulations for as much as a decade from Republicans’ reconciliation package marked Silicon Valley’s first major loss of the second Trump administration. But the episode was only “a prelude to future battles around who gets to write the rulebook on a technology that is rapidly remaking the economy,” POLITICO ’s Chase DiFeliciantonio writes.

— “The main driver of the measure, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz , has threatened to bring the measure back , suggesting the fight is far from over. … The freeze became a rallying cry for much of the tech industry and their moneyed backers, who have long argued a patchwork of state AI rules will hobble the United States’ ability to compete with rivals like China when it comes to the technology — an argument that has resonated with the Trump administration and its MAGA allies.”

GAMING INDUSTRY PIVOTS TO TAX FIX: The gaming industry is falling in line behind a bipartisan measure aimed at addressing a tax change in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that sparked a last-minute outcry from gamblers. Earlier this week, Las Vegas Democratic Rep. Dina Titus introduced legislation that would restore a provision allowing gamblers to write off 100 percent of their losses, which the GOP megabill signed into law last week would cap at 90 percent.
section_heading: GAMING INDUSTRY PIVOTS TO TAX FIX

context_text: — The National Thoroughbred Racing Association , which protested the tax change just as the reconciliation bill neared the finish line last week, threw its support behind Titus’ fix, calling the deduction cap “detrimental” to bettors who are foundational to horse racing and pledging to work with the Trump administration and Congress to address the matter.
section_heading: GAMING INDUSTRY PIVOTS TO TAX FIX

context_text: — Titus’ bill has already drawn support from across the aisle, with GOP Reps. Troy Nehls (Texas), Mark Amodei (Nev.) and Jeff Van Drew (N.J.) — all of whom voted for the reconciliation bill containing the tax change — signing on as cosponsors. Titus’ fellow Democratic Reps. Ro Khanna (Calif.) and Steven Horsford (Nev.) are also backing the bill, though the gaming industry source argued that the best shot for a fix will likely involve hitching a ride on some as-yet determined legislative vehicle.
section_heading: GAMING INDUSTRY PIVOTS TO TAX FIX

context_text: — The American Gaming Association , which listed the extension of the 100 percent deduction as one of its top priorities for the reconciliation bill in a memo to lawmakers in May, said in a statement praising the overall bill following its passage that it would work to “restore the long-standing tax treatment of gaming losses” and supports Titus’ fix.

DEMS TARGET LIBRARY DONATIONS: More than two dozen congressional Democrats have signed on to a new bill aimed at injecting transparency into funding for presidential libraries — a move that comes as President Donald Trump rakes in tens of millions of dollars in pledges from corporations whose business Trump has immense say over.

— Unlike with fundraising for political campaigns, there are virtually no restrictions on when and how presidents can raise money for their libraries. And there are no disclosure requirements apart from the rules that govern all tax-exempt nonprofits. That makes the endeavor rife with ethics concerns, according to Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), the co-authors of the Presidential Library Anti-Corruptio

— The bill would ban presidents from raising money for their future library (except from 501(c)3 groups) while in office, which the lawmakers note was the standard adopted by the Obama Foundation . There would be an additional two-year cooling off period for donations from foreign nationals, lobbyists, contractors and pardon seekers, and a ban on straw donations.

— The measure, of course, won’t be going anywhere in the GOP-controlled Congress. But a report from Warren’s office this week found that less than six months into Trump’s second term, his library coffers are already flush with commitments of at least $63 million, thanks to eight-figure settlement payments from companies like Paramount , ABC and Meta .

FIRST IN PI: Checkmate Government Affairs is opening its first international office in Tokyo, a notable expansion for a lobbying firm that set up shop in D.C. just seven months ago. Former Japanese politician Takeo Kawamura , who served as a top adviser to a former Japanese prime minister and now works with top Japanese and Korean companies in the private sector, will be the chair of Checkmate Japan.

— While an international expansion was always a possibility for the North Carolina-based firm — which has seen an explosion of domestic and foreign lobbying business thanks in part to its inroads with Trumpworld — it was Kawamura and his team who approached Checkmate about the idea first, according to Chris LaCivita Jr.

K STREET’S IVY LEAGUE PAYDAY: Ivy League universities in President Donald Trump ‘s crosshairs poured record sums into lobbying during the first six months of Trump’s second term, according to a PI anaylsis of disclosures filed this week. Cornell University led the Ivies with $444,000 in lobbying expenditures last quarter — a 90 percent increase from what the university spent from January through March of this year, and the most ever for the school in a single quarter.

— The Ivies’ second-biggest spender, Yale University , reported $320,000 in lobbying expenditures last quarter — nearly double what it spent during the same period a year ago. It’s a nearly 30 percent increase compared to Yale’s lobbying outlays during the first three months of the year.

— Yale’s lobbying effort included bringing on two of K Street’s most prominent lobbying shops, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld . The firms supplied Yale with a roster of hired guns that includes a former GOP member of Congress, one of Trump’s former personal lawyers and a top Republican fundraiser.

— “Nine of the groups that signed the letter have received funding from Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America , better known as PhRMA, the primary trade organization representing the pharmaceutical industry. — “Many of the organizations signing the letter have pulled in six-figure sums from PhRMA,” including the Trade Alliance to Promote Prosperity , American Commitment , Competitive Enterprise Institute , Consumer Action for a Strong Economy , and the Council for Citizens Against Government Waste . — So it should be no surprise that the restaurant, which recently earned a spot on The Washington Post ’s list of the city’s top 20 newcomers , has also become a destination for GOP campaigns and political groups. They have disclosed almost $45,000 in spending at Butterworth’s since last year, according to campaign finance reports.

— The restaurant’s top campaign patron so far is the governance-focused Tuesday Group . The group’s PAC shelled out $21,000 across three different occasions for event venue and food and beverage, according to FEC filings. The leadership PAC for first-term Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska) reported $12,000 in disbursements for event rental and catering at Butterworth’s in December and January, filings show.

— Also among the top spenders was a joint fundraising committee for Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas), which reported spending $6,300 for “event catering” for fundraising purposes on Jan. 3, and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , whose campaign committee reported spending $4,500 on catering and facility rental and food and beverage on three separate occasions in March and May.
— Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Reps. Harriett Hageman (R-Wyo.) and Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) have also reported campaign expenses at Butterworth’s in the first half of this year, along with the RNC .

— Lawmakers like Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) have pitched the reforms for inclusion in the NDAA later this year. But defense groups have argued that limitations on the program, which works to foster breakthroughs in advanced defense technology — particularly among small or emerging firms — could stifle innovation in the sector. The industry coalition is planning a fly-in next month, as well as a digital ad campaign, to take its case directly to the Hill.

— White House chief of staff Susie Wiles spoke highly of Morse’s new venture in an interview, calling him “an important and integral part of the successes we’ve had.” A former lobbyist herself, Wiles told PI that clients are clamoring for “some guidance about the process and some strategic … counsel” about decoding the Trump administration. “And nobody is better able to do that” than Morse, she said.

— Will Moschella , who co-leads Brownstein’s government relations practice, echoed Wiles’ assessment of Morse. “He’s going to provide what I think is going to be unrivaled insight into the way the president’s team is thinking about issues,” he told PI. “He’s been in the middle of a lot of important debates, and knows a lot of the key players throughout the administration, particularly in the agencies, and he’ll be helpful in providing those insights to our clients.”

— This isn’t Morse’s first stint as a lobbyist. After stints at HHS, HUD and DOT during Trump’s first term, Morse went to work at Wiles’ former haunt Ballard Partners , before eventually joining her at Mercury Public Affairs . Morse has been working with Trump’s team for the past year — first heading up external and GOP outreach for last year’s Republican National Convention in Milwaukee and then working for the transition team.

GELLIE LANDS AT PILLSBURY: Jennifer Gellie , who steered the Justice Department’s FARA Unit during a pivotal moment in DOJ’s crackdown on illicit foreign influence campaigns, has joined the white shoe law and lobbying firm Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman as a partner in the international trade group.

— “Jennifer’s arrival comes at a time when being able to understand and adapt to evolving U.S. sanctions and export control policies is absolutely essential to U.S. and multinational companies as well as those based outside the U.S.,” Pillsbury Chair David Dekker said in a statement, touting Gellie as “uniquely qualified to guide clients through high-risk, high-profile national security issues.”

— Gellie left DOJ in July after nearly a decade at the department, during which she spent almost three years as head of the FARA Unit before being tapped to lead the Counterintelligence and Export Control Section. Under Gellie, DOJ continued the aggressive enforcement posture toward foreign lobbying violations that began under former special counsel Robert Mueller and Gellie’s predecessor Brandon Van Grack .

— Simpson will take over as ACU’s president and CEO in November from the group’s longtime leader, former Rep. Jim Nussle , who announced his retirement in April. The addition of TDY, which opened almost two decades ago, will grow the headcount of the combined firm’s health policy team to more than 50.
— “In the world of health care policy, their founders, partners and expertise are best in class. Full Stop,” Joel Johnson , who leads FGS’ D.C. office, told PI in a statement.

—  “Health care organizations face unprecedented, interconnected challenges, from regulatory shifts to reputational risks,” Kim James , the leader of FGS’ North America health practice, said in a statement. “Now more than ever, they need a single, integrated partner who can navigate the full spectrum of policy, communications and stakeholder dynamics.”

COATS TO LIBERTY PARTNERS GROUP : Former senator and director of national intelligence Dan Coats has joined Liberty Partners Group as a senior policy advisor, the firm announced yesterday. Coats will be the third former senator in the firm after founder Connie Mack and Debbie Stabenow.

FLYING IN: Despite the shutdown, fly-ins are still taking place on the Hill, including for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce , which wrapped up a three-day fly-in with small business leaders today. Business owners had more than three dozen meetings with House and Senate offices, during which they called for an end to the shutdown and the passage of permitting reform and thanked Republicans for passing tax cuts.

— Also on the Hill this week was t he American Society of Travel Advisors . Hundreds of travel advisors and industry advocates came to Washington as part of the group’s annual Legislative Day to meet with lawmakers about small business protections and consumer-friendly travel policies.

— Meanwhile the National Retail Federation was on the Hill today with 15 small retailers as part of the trade group’s sixth tariff-focused fly-in since Trump rolled out his so-called reciprocal tariffs in April.

CHAMBER OF PROGRESS EYES STATEHOUSES: Liberal-leaning tech lobbying group Chamber of Progress is launching a new influence initiative to shape how Democratic statehouses approach AI regulation.

— The group’s new State AI Leadership Project, or SAIL, is in large part a response to the recent flood of state legislation related to AI — itself a function of the deepening tech-policy paralysis in Washington. “We, just like many other organizations, are supportive of a federal framework, but it’s very clear states are not waiting,” said Koustubh “K.J.” Bagchi , head of U.S. policy and government relations at Chamber of Progress and leader of the new initiative.

— Chamber of Progress is funded by AI industry heavyweights like Google , Andreessen Horowitz and Nvidia — companies that have all worked to limit the political influence of individuals and organizations worried about AI risks. The group’s new SAIL initiative aims to extend that work into blue states, where legislators have recently advanced bills that would impose new safety frameworks and other restrictions on the technology.

KILLING HIM SOFTLY: Pras Michel, founding member of 90s hip-hop trio The Fugees, was sentenced to 14 years in prison today following a conviction on charges that he acted as an unregistered foreign agent of China, made illegal campaign contributions using foreign money and later tried to cover it up.

— Jurors convicted Michel, 52, in 2023 on 10 felony counts related to two schemes hatched by Michel and a Malaysian businessman, Jho Low , who is separately accused of embezzling billions of dollars from that country’s sovereign wealth fund.

— Michel’s trial was punctuated by testimony from star witnesses Leonardo DiCaprio , Jeff Sessions and Michel himself. Jurors heard details of the schemes, carried out by Michel and others and funded by Low, who used the billions he allegedly stole from Malaysia’s 1MDB fund to lead a glamorous lifestyle, praying with celebrities around the globe. Low used some of the money he allegedly stole to fund Hollywood films, including DiCaprio’s Wolf of Wall Street.

— The first scheme involved an attempt to secure a meeting between Low and President Barack Obama so Low could get a picture of himself shaking the president’s hand. Michel, using money obtained from Low, donated nearly $2 million to a super PAC supporting Obama’s 2012 reelection campaign and hid the source of the money using a network of straw donors.

— The second scheme involved efforts by Michel, Republican fundraiser Elliott Broidy and others to lobby the first Trump Justice Department to drop an ongoing investigation into Low related to the 1MDB scandal. Low was indicted along with Michel but remains a fugitive in China.

— In addition to pushing for the DOJ to drop its investigation of Low, Michel and Broidy also took money from Low to lobby the Trump administration on behalf of China, pushing for officials to extradite a Chinese dissident living in New York. That dissident, Guo Wengui , was later arrested and convicted in his own fraud case. He has not yet been sentenced.

— “The sentence reflects the gravity of the defendant’s efforts to manipulate decision-making at the highest levels of our government, for profit and on behalf of foreign interests,” said John Keller , a former prosecutor on the case who resigned in February when he was ordered to dismiss the case against New York Mayor Eric Adams.

JOURNEY TO THE MANOSPHERE: The 2024 elections shined a spotlight on the widening political gap between men and women, vaulting terms like “manosphere” into the popular lexicon. And as Democrats have scrambled to find their way out of the political wilderness — in large part by trying to boost the party’s appeal to men — the progressive consultancy Precision Strategies is out with new research it hopes can help.
— In partnership with Tunnl , Precision has developed the “Manosphere Index” to provide campaigns and brands with insight into how to reach men by diving into what is shaping their worldview.

— Post-2024, “there was a lot of data and framing that very narrowly talked about this ‘masculinity crisis,’” said Krishana Davis, who leads Precision’s digital and multicultural engagement efforts. But much of that dialogue was “flattening the conversation, and basically looking at millions of men from a very monolithic view.” Or, she argued, it became “a shorthand of white men, when even white men are not a monolith.”

— Through thousands of interviews, Precision and Tunnl found that economic pressures, more than ideology, are shaping masculinity today. Religion is also playing a major role in men’s lives, especially among Gen Z, Davis said, with many finding a sense of community in faith in addition to platforms like YouTube and various podcasts rather than more traditional media institutions.

IN RELATED NEWS: Some of the biggest names in prediction markets have apparently decided they don’t need the AGA and have launched a new coalition to better represent their interests in Washington, Nathan Bomey scoops for Axios .

— Kalshi , Crypto.com , Robinhood , Coinbase and Underdog are the founding members of the new Coalition for Prediction Markets , which will focus on promoting federal regulation of the prediction business and oppose state regulatory efforts.

NEW LAWSUIT SEEKS RECORDS ON BIG LAW DEALS: Government watchdog group American Oversight announced today that it has filed a FOIA lawsuit against the Commerce and Justice Departments seeking records related to the Trump administration’s deals with nine major law firms.

— The lawsuit seeks “communications, agreements, ethics waivers, billing records and legal analyses” related to work the firms have done for the administration. At least three firms — Paul Weiss , Kirkland & Ellis and Simpson Thacher — have reportedly assisted the Commerce Department with trade deals.

FIRST IN PI — CAPITOL HILL CELEBRATES JENNER & BLOCK: Congressional Republicans and Democrats came together last night for a bipartisan event celebrating the release of “ When Congress Comes Calling ,” a newly updated handbook on congressional investigations published by Jenner & Block and the Project on Government Oversight .

— Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), two of the president’s staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, were part of the crowd at the event, which celebrated the work of the government watchdog group and a law firm President Donald Trump previously accused of abusing its pro-bono practice to “engage in activities that undermine justice and the interests of the United States.”

— Jenner is one of four law firms that sued the Trump administration earlier this year in response to executive orders threatening their ability to do business. The order targeting Jenner accused the firm of engaging in “obvious partisan representations to achieve political ends.” It cited its previous hiring of former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann as justification for suspending security clearances held by firm lawyers, reviewing government contracts held by the firm and its clients and l

— But you wouldn’t detect any of that from the tenor of last night’s event, which brought Johnson and Jordan together with Democrats like Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.), per a tipster.

— “This edition of ‘When Congress Comes Calling’ will serve as a go-to guide for congressional investigators for years to come, and we’d like to thank the Project on Government Oversight for entrusting us with the responsibility of updating this seminal publication,” said Ashley Callen , co-chair of Jenner’s congressional investigations practice.

ARIZONA CITY SAYS NO TO AI: A push to build a data center in Chandler, Arizona, came to an end yesterday after city officials voted to deny a developer’s request to rezone a plot of land that currently houses an abandoned office building. The effort gained national attention after former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema began lobbying for the data center, appearing at multiple local board meetings on behalf of the AI Infrastructure Coalition , Jason Plautz reports for E&E News .

UNLEASH THE WALL STREET EXECS: Lobbyists for banks and cryptocurrency companies have been brawling for months over a landmark bill that would overhaul how digital assets are regulated. Now, bank CEOs from around the country are about to wade into the fight, per our friends at Morning Money .

— The clash centers on whether crypto exchanges should be allowed to pay an annual percentage yield via rewards programs to customers who hold stablecoins. In a new twist, the American Bankers Association is now trying to harness the political capital of its members by urging bank leaders to press lawmakers for bill language that would ban crypto exchanges from doing so.

— The issue “demands immediate action from every bank leader in the country,” ABA President Rob Nichols wrote in a letter to CEOs . “We need you — along with your staff and, where appropriate, your customers — to contact Congress and make our voices heard.”

A coalition of crypto companies led by the Blockchain Association wrote in a letter to senators last month that proposals to crack down on exchanges’ rewards programs “would reopen a settled issue, undermine a carefully negotiated compromise, reduce consumer choice, suppress competition, and inject uncertainty into the implementation of a new law before regulations have even been proposed.”

FLYING IN: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce hit the Hill today with more than 50 business and association leaders to try to regain momentum for a permitting overhaul after the House passed a package of reforms before skipping town last year.

— A policy forum this morning featured remarks from Senate Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.), Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) and Emily Domenech , who chairs the Trump administration’s permitting council. FIRST IN PI : North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley has praised the Trump administration for its ouster of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro , calling it “a very important step.” He said he was “so proud” of how Delta Force handled his capture, Daniel L. reports.

— What Whatley didn’t mention is that he and his family have up to a million plus dollars invested in three major oil companies that saw spikes in their shares after President Donald Trump said he would increase oil production in Venezuela, according to his personal financial disclosure filed in late November.

BONDI’S BIG FARA MOVE: In one of her first moves as the nation’s top prosecutor on Wednesday, Attorney General Pam Bondi outlined a sea change in how her Justice Department plans to approach foreign influence campaigns in the U.S., moving to crackdown on enforcing foreign agent laws that have been ramping up for close to a decade now.

1. Does this mean a foreign lobbying free-for-all? Probably not. Bondi’s directive limiting criminal prosecutions to “similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors” certainly may shift DOJ’s focus away from PR teams, lobbyists and consultants engaged in behind-the-scenes influence peddling and covert propaganda efforts on behalf of foreign clients.
